lines: Notice what I held fixed on purpose: the cluster size, the data, the query text. Only the finishing time changed.
When everything obvious is held constant and the result still differs, the explanation has to be in how the work gets executed, not what hardware it's sitting on.
Before I answer, think back to the vectorization lesson you've already seen. One engine handles a row, finishes it, moves to the next. The other handles a whole batch of rows at once.
Which approach do you think modern hardware actually rewards?
answer: Vectorized batches. Modern processors are built to chew through many similar operations at once, and row-at-a-time execution leaves most of that capability unused.
This isn't a new idea — it's the same lesson from earlier in the course, now with a name, a vendor, and a native implementation behind it.

lines: Resist the urge to sort these into 'fast' and 'slow.' The real difference is what happens to each one between jobs.
One sits and waits for the next job to show up. One disappears the second its job ends. One never touches your own cloud account at all.
Watch the two totals diverge even though both ran the exact same four jobs. The job-compute total only counts work. The all-purpose total counts the waiting, too.
Forty-five minutes of difference, on four short jobs in one day — and nothing about the jobs themselves explains it.
This number didn't come from a demo cherry-picked to look good. It's the vendor's own published benchmark, on a standard industry test, compared against its own prior runtime.
And notice the range below it: real customers, on their own workloads, seeing even more.
Here's the nuance worth catching: the pool saves you time, and it saves you the platform's own unit charge — but the underlying machine is still rented from somewhere, and that meter doesn't stop.
A pool moves cost around. It doesn't make idle time free.
Think about why the driver specifically never goes on spot pricing. Lose a worker, and the cluster just has less capacity for a moment. Lose the driver, and the whole cluster is gone.
That's not a cost rule. That's a reliability rule wearing a pricing label.
If you only remember one line: there is no such thing as 'the DBU rate.' There's a published list, and it has a different number on every row.
Asking 'how many DBUs' without naming which compute type is like asking the price of 'a seat' without saying which airline.
If you only remember one line: four compute types means four different bills for the exact same job, and the difference is never about raw speed.
Photon proves the vectorization lesson shipped as real code. The DBU proves 'one price' was never true to begin with.
Before I answer, notice what makes this job hard to plan around: it's short, it's rare, and nobody knows exactly when it'll run.
Which compute type punishes unpredictability the least?
answer: Job compute. It doesn't care when the job shows up, because it's created fresh for that one run and torn down the second it's done.
All-purpose compute would need someone babysitting a schedule just to avoid paying for days of silence between runs — exactly the cost this topic already measured.
